catalog_quote: ACCENTUATION. — Les différents accents : ouvert, fermé, long, bref, nasal, tonique qui se divise lui-même en accent tonique proprement dit, en accent de hauteur, jouent le plus grand rôle dans l'intelligibilité de cette langue. Il importe donc de les bien observer et de ne pas les confondre. ACCENT TONIQUE. — L'accent tonique consiste dans un ' coup de voix ' sans élévation sensible du ton. La syllabe qui le porte est prononcée avec plus d'intensité ou d'effort. Il se trouve ordinairement sur la première syllabe non affectée du signe de brièveté. ACCENT DE HAUTEUR. — L'accent de hauteur consiste dans une élévation du ton, soit sur un mot monosyllabique, soit sur une ou plusieurs syllabes du même mot. Il est indiqué par un accent aigu placé sur la syllabe accentuée. REMARQUE. — Le n° 1 désigne le Gmbwaĝa, le n° 2 le Gbanziri, le n° 3 le Mõnjõmbo. [p. 6, '3. Voyelles', in three columns:] …

new_statements.translation: Accentuation. — The various accents: open, closed, long, short, nasal, tonic (which itself divides into the tonic accent proper and the pitch accent) play the greatest role in the intelligibility of this language. [...] Tonic accent. — The tonic accent consists of a 'stroke of the voice' without any noticeable raising of pitch. The syllable bearing it is pronounced with more intensity or effort. It is ordinarily found on the first syllable not marked with the sign of shortness. Pitch accent. — The pitch accent consists of a raising of pitch, either on a monosyllabic word or on one or more syllables of the same word. It is indicated by an acute accent placed on the accented syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Intensity stress ('accent tonique') falls ordinarily on the first syllable of the word, skipping any syllable marked as short (breve); pitch ('accent de hauteur', i.e. tone, marked with an acute) is treated as a separate, independent property that may sit on any syllable(s). So: initial stress, weight-hedged by a short-vowel skipping clause, alongside lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'ordinairement' and the clause that syllables marked with the breve (short) sign do not take the stress; no further exceptions. The same paragraph is a template reused across Calloc'h's 1911 vocabularies (Gbéa volume: 'en règle générale sur la pénultième non affectée du signe de brièveté'), so the shortness clause is formulaic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a combined grammar sketch of Gmbwaga, Gbanziri and Monjombo ('cette langue'); citation-form vocabulary; impressionistic missionary description from 1911 with no examples marked for stress (only pitch is marked in the vocabulary, by acute accents). Modern descriptions treat Gbanzili as a register-tone language and are silent on stress in the parts accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Calloc'h 1911) is a combined missionary sketch of three varieties it calls 'trois dialectes d'une même langue' spoken on the Ubangi: Gmbwaga (= the 'Bondjo' riverine variety, not Gbanziri proper), Gbanziri, and Monjombo (= Monzombo, monz1249). The accentuation paragraph is written once for 'cette langue' and is not language-specific to Gbanziri; the numbered forms (1 = Gmbwaga, 2 = Gbanziri, 3 = Monjombo) in the examples show the three are treated as one grammar. It is also an authorial template: the identical paragraph appears in Calloc'h's 1911 Gbéa volume with 'pénultième' in place of 'première syllabe' (held under alii1240), so only the position word is language-specific. Modern work (Rombi & Thomas 2006; Rombi 1994; Boyeldieu 2013) treats Gbanzili as a register-tone language (high vs low, low realised low or mid; tonal schemes mark verbal aspect) and none of the accessible modern texts mentions stress. Gbanzili and 'Bôlaka/Buraka are two little-differentiated variants of one language (Boyeldieu 2013: 1), matching the Glottolog languoid.
